evidence.title: Prediction of Automotive Wire Harness Aging Based on CNN-biLSTM-Attention.
evidence.abstract: Under the transition towards electrification and intelligence in modern automotive industry, the health status of low-voltage wiring harnesses directly affects vehicle performance and safety. To address the challenge of predicting performance degradation caused by multi-physics coupling effects during wiring harness aging, this study proposes a CNN-BiLSTM-Attention hybrid neural network model. By capturing voltage, current, and temperature parameters during low-voltage system operation, the model combines CNN's local feature extraction, BiLSTM's temporal sequence analysis, and attention mechanisms to predict aging levels. Accelerated aging experiments were conducted to obtain wiring harnesses with different degradation levels from new to 720 h aged states, and a dedicated experimental platform was built for data collection and verification. The results show the system achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.02806, with 32.50% and 62.06% error reduction compared to LSTM and Random Forest models, respectively, demonstrating effective prediction performance.

evidence.title: Battery electronification: intracell actuation and thermal management.
evidence.abstract: Electrochemical batteries - essential to vehicle electrification and renewable energy storage - have ever-present reaction interfaces that require compromise among power, energy, lifetime, and safety. Here we report a chip-in-cell battery by integrating an ultrathin foil heater and a microswitch into the layer-by-layer architecture of a battery cell to harness intracell actuation and mutual thermal management between the heat-generating switch and heat-absorbing battery materials. The result is a two-terminal, drop-in ready battery with no bulky heat sinks or heavy wiring needed for an external high-power switch. We demonstrate rapid self-heating (∼ 60 °C min - 1 ), low energy consumption (0.138% °C - 1 of battery energy), and excellent durability (> 2000 cycles) of the greatly simplified chip-in-cell structure. The battery electronification platform unveiled here opens doors to include integrated-circuit chips inside energy storage cells for sensing, control, actuating, and wireless communications such that performance, lifetime, and safety of electrochemical energy storage devices can be internally regulated.

evidence.title: Development of an Energy Efficient and Cost Effective Autonomous Vehicle Research Platform.
evidence.abstract: Commercialization of autonomous vehicle technology is a major goal of the automotive industry, thus research in this space is rapidly expanding across the world. However, despite this high level of research activity, literature detailing a straightforward and cost-effective approach to the development of an AV research platform is sparse. To address this need, we present the methodology and results regarding the AV instrumentation and controls of a 2019 Kia Niro which was developed for a local AV pilot program. This platform includes a drive-by-wire actuation kit, Aptiv electronically scanning radar, stereo camera, MobilEye computer vision system, LiDAR, inertial measurement unit, two global positioning system receivers to provide heading information, and an in-vehicle computer for driving environment perception and path planning. Robotic Operating System software is used as the system middleware between the instruments and the autonomous application algorithms. After selection, installation, and integration of these components, our results show successful utilization of all sensors, drive-by-wire functionality, a total additional power* consumption of 242.8 Watts (*Typical), and an overall cost of $118,189 USD, which is a significant saving compared to other commercially available systems with similar functionality. This vehicle continues to serve as our primary AV research and development platform.

evidence.title: Control Barrier Functions for Shared Control and Vehicle Safety
evidence.abstract: This manuscript presents a control barrier function based approach to shared control for preventing a vehicle from entering the part of the state space where it is unrecoverable. The maximal phase recoverable ellipse is presented as a safe set in the sideslip angle--yaw rate phase plane where the vehicle's state can be maintained. An exponential control barrier function is then defined on the maximal phase recoverable ellipse to promote safety. Simulations demonstrate that this approach enables safe drifting, that is, driving at the handling limit without spinning out. Results are then validated for shared control drifting with an experimental vehicle in a closed course. The results show the ability of this shared control formulation to maintain the vehicle's state within a safe domain in a computationally efficient manner, even in extreme drifting maneuvers.

evidence.title: Distributed Nonlinear Model Predictive Control and Metric Learning for Heterogeneous Vehicle Platooning with Cut-in/Cut-out Maneuvers
evidence.abstract: Vehicle platooning has been shown to be quite fruitful in the transportation industry to enhance fuel economy, road throughput, and driving comfort. Model Predictive Control (MPC) is widely used in literature for platoon control to achieve certain objectives, such as safely reducing the distance among consecutive vehicles while following the leader vehicle. In this paper, we propose a Distributed Nonlinear MPC (DNMPC), based upon an existing approach, to control a heterogeneous dynamic platoon with unidirectional topologies, handling possible cut-in/cut-out maneuvers. The introduced method addresses a collision-free driving experience while tracking the desired speed profile and maintaining a safe desired gap among the vehicles. The time of convergence in the dynamic platooning is derived based on the time of cut-in and/or cut-out maneuvers. In addition, we analyze the improvement level of driving comfort, fuel economy, and absolute and relative convergence of the method by using distributed metric learning and distributed optimization with Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM). Simulation results on a dynamic platoon with cut-in and cut-out maneuvers and with different unidirectional topologies show the effectiveness of the introduced method.

evidence.title: Exponential input-to-state stabilization of a class of diagonal boundary control systems with delay boundary control
evidence.abstract: This paper deals with the exponential input-to-state stabilization with respect to boundary disturbances of a class of diagonal infinite-dimensional systems via delay boundary control. The considered input delays are uncertain and time-varying. The proposed control strategy consists of a constant-delay predictor feedback controller designed on a truncated finite-dimensional model capturing the unstable modes of the original infinite-dimensional system. We show that the resulting closed-loop system is exponentially input-to-state stable with fading memory of both additive boundary input perturbations and disturbances in the computation of the predictor feedback.

evidence.abstract:
Over the last forty years, the use of electronic controls within the automotive industry

has grown considerably. In-vehicle network technologies such as the Controller Area

Network (CAN) and Local Interconnect Network (LIN) are used to connect

Electronic Control Units (ECU) together, mainly to reduce the amount of wiring that

would be required if hardwired integration were used.

Modern passenger cars contain many networks, which means that for the

architecture designer, there is an almost overwhelming number of choices on how to

design/partition the system depending on factors such as cost, weight, availability of

ECUs, safety, Electro-Magnetic Compatibility (EMC) etc. Despite the increasing role

played by in-vehicle networks in automotive electrical architectures, its design could

currently be described as a “black art”. Not only is there an almost overwhelming

number of choices facing the designer, but there is currently a lack of a quantifiable

process to aid decision making and there is a dearth of published literature available.

NetGen is a software tool used to design CAN/J1939, LIN and FlexRay

networks. For the product to remain competitive, it is desirable to have novel features

over the competition. This report describes a body of work, the aim of which was to

research in-vehicle network design processes, and to provide an improvement to such

processes. The opportunities of customer projects and availability of customer

information resulted in the scope of the research focusing on the adoption of LIN

technology and whether the adoption of it could reduce the cost and weight of the

target architecture. The research can therefore be seen to address two issues: firstly

the general problem of network designers needing to design in-vehicle network based

system.value: Prediction of Automotive Wire Harness Aging Based on CNN-biLSTM-Attention.

abstract.value: Under the transition towards electrification and intelligence in modern automotive industry, the health status of low-voltage wiring harnesses directly affects vehicle performance and safety. To address the challenge of predicting performance degradation caused by multi-physics coupling effects during wiring harness aging, this study proposes a CNN-BiLSTM-Attention hybrid neural network model. By capturing voltage, current, and temperature parameters during low-voltage system operation, the model combines CNN's local feature extraction, BiLSTM's temporal sequence analysis, and attention mechanisms to predict aging levels. Accelerated aging experiments were conducted to obtain wiring harnesses with different degradation levels from new to 720 h aged states, and a dedicated experimental platform was built for data collection and verification. The results show the system achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.02806, with 32.50% and 62.06% error reduction compared to LSTM and Random Forest models, respectively, demonstrating effective prediction performance.

system.value: Battery electronification: intracell actuation and thermal management.

abstract.value: Electrochemical batteries - essential to vehicle electrification and renewable energy storage - have ever-present reaction interfaces that require compromise among power, energy, lifetime, and safety. Here we report a chip-in-cell battery by integrating an ultrathin foil heater and a microswitch into the layer-by-layer architecture of a battery cell to harness intracell actuation and mutual thermal management between the heat-generating switch and heat-absorbing battery materials. The result is a two-terminal, drop-in ready battery with no bulky heat sinks or heavy wiring needed for an external high-power switch. We demonstrate rapid self-heating (∼ 60 °C min - 1 ), low energy consumption (0.138% °C - 1 of battery energy), and excellent durability (> 2000 cycles) of the greatly simplified chip-in-cell structure. The battery electronification platform unveiled here opens doors to include integrated-circuit chips inside energy storage cells for sensing, control, actuating, and wireless communications such that performance, lifetime, and safety of electrochemical energy storage devices can be internally regulated.

system.value: Development of an Energy Efficient and Cost Effective Autonomous Vehicle Research Platform.

abstract.value: Commercialization of autonomous vehicle technology is a major goal of the automotive industry, thus research in this space is rapidly expanding across the world. However, despite this high level of research activity, literature detailing a straightforward and cost-effective approach to the development of an AV research platform is sparse. To address this need, we present the methodology and results regarding the AV instrumentation and controls of a 2019 Kia Niro which was developed for a local AV pilot program. This platform includes a drive-by-wire actuation kit, Aptiv electronically scanning radar, stereo camera, MobilEye computer vision system, LiDAR, inertial measurement unit, two global positioning system receivers to provide heading information, and an in-vehicle computer for driving environment perception and path planning. Robotic Operating System software is used as the system middleware between the instruments and the autonomous application algorithms. After selection, installation, and integration of these components, our results show successful utilization of all sensors, drive-by-wire functionality, a total additional power* consumption of 242.8 Watts (*Typical), and an overall cost of $118,189 USD, which is a significant saving compared to other commercially available systems with similar functionality. This vehicle continues to serve as our primary AV research and development platform.

system.value: Control Barrier Functions for Shared Control and Vehicle Safety

abstract.value: This manuscript presents a control barrier function based approach to shared control for preventing a vehicle from entering the part of the state space where it is unrecoverable. The maximal phase recoverable ellipse is presented as a safe set in the sideslip angle--yaw rate phase plane where the vehicle's state can be maintained. An exponential control barrier function is then defined on the maximal phase recoverable ellipse to promote safety. Simulations demonstrate that this approach enables safe drifting, that is, driving at the handling limit without spinning out. Results are then validated for shared control drifting with an experimental vehicle in a closed course. The results show the ability of this shared control formulation to maintain the vehicle's state within a safe domain in a computationally efficient manner, even in extreme drifting maneuvers.

system.value: Distributed Nonlinear Model Predictive Control and Metric Learning for Heterogeneous Vehicle Platooning with Cut-in/Cut-out Maneuvers

abstract.value: Vehicle platooning has been shown to be quite fruitful in the transportation industry to enhance fuel economy, road throughput, and driving comfort. Model Predictive Control (MPC) is widely used in literature for platoon control to achieve certain objectives, such as safely reducing the distance among consecutive vehicles while following the leader vehicle. In this paper, we propose a Distributed Nonlinear MPC (DNMPC), based upon an existing approach, to control a heterogeneous dynamic platoon with unidirectional topologies, handling possible cut-in/cut-out maneuvers. The introduced method addresses a collision-free driving experience while tracking the desired speed profile and maintaining a safe desired gap among the vehicles. The time of convergence in the dynamic platooning is derived based on the time of cut-in and/or cut-out maneuvers. In addition, we analyze the improvement level of driving comfort, fuel economy, and absolute and relative convergence of the method by using distributed metric learning and distributed optimization with Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM). Simulation results on a dynamic platoon with cut-in and cut-out maneuvers and with different unidirectional topologies show the effectiveness of the introduced method.

system.value: A novel optimization methodology of modular wiring harnesses in modern vehicles : weight reduction and safe operation

abstract.value: The weight of electric and electronic components of cars has been uninterruptedly increasing through the last decades, and thus the weight of their wiring harnesses. This fact has awakened the interest of car manufacturers on the weight and cost optimization of automotive wiring harnesses . For this reason, this dissertation discusses and develops approaches to reduce the amount of copper for the purpose of current conduction, i.e. the cross-sections of all of the wires of the car, without endangering safety. On the one hand, harnesses must withstand continuous operation currents. On account of this, it is necessary to know the characteristic flow of current of the in-vehicle electrical network. Nevertheless. the huge quantity of available combinations of equipment of the car produces a proportional variety of customer-specific wiring hamesses, and makes it unfeasible to simulate all of them. This thesis points attention on specific segments of the wiring harnesses. Sorne of them can have many possible compositions, which are related to the customer's car settings. Since computation time is a limiting factor here, it is proposed to predict the bundle heating behaviors by means of response surfaces, obtained from a set of finite element simulation results and the least squares method. On the other hand, the correct wire sizes must ensure that they are protected by their associated melting fuses, so that their maximum acceptable temperature is not exceeded after short circuits. Since many wires in cars are connected to other wires with splices, or may suffer short-circuits in their electric loads, these short-circuits can flow across different wires. In modular wiring harnesses, each of the wires can have different lengths and different installation ratios, their cross-section affects the cost of the wire harness with different importance, as well as the short circuit and the final temperature of the wire. The finite volume method is used to simulate the short circuit of series-connected wires. Finally, non-linear optimization is used to find the mínimum cross­ sections of wires respecting the constraints of maximum temperature and mínimum short-circuit current. abstract.value: As part of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA’s) continuing assessment of advanced light-duty automotive technologies in support of regulatory and compliance programs, a 2018 Toyota Camry front wheel drive eight-speed automatic transmission was benchmarked. Te benchmarking data were used as inputs to EPA’s Advanced Light-duty Powertrain and Hybrid Analysis (ALPHA) vehicle simulation model to estimate GHG emissions from lightduty vehicles. ALPHA requires both detailed engine fuel consumption maps and transmission torque loss maps. EPA’s National Vehicle and Fuels Emissions Laboratory has developed a streamlined, cost-efective in-house method of transmission testing, capable of gathering a dataset sufcient to characterize transmissions within ALPHA. Tis testing methodology targets the range of transmission operation observed during vehicle testing over EPA’s city and highway drive cycles. Introduction and Background The National Center for Advanced Technology (NCAT), part of EPA’s National Vehicle and Fuel Emissions Laboratory, leads a team that assesses the efectiveness of advanced low emission and low fuel consumption technologies by benchmarking a broad range of key light-duty vehicles, engines and transmissions. Te NCAT team benchmarks advanced technologies using laboratory test methods to characterize engine controls, fuel consumption, emissions, and component losses [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. NCAT leverages in-depth, detailed engineering analyses along with extensive engine and chassis dynamometer laboratory testing to evaluate advanced vehicle, engine and transmission technologies. system.value: Design of in-vehicle networked control system architectures through the use of new design to cost and weight processes : innovation report

abstract.value:
Over the last forty years, the use of electronic controls within the automotive industry

has grown considerably. In-vehicle network technologies such as the Controller Area

Network (CAN) and Local Interconnect Network (LIN) are used to connect

Electronic Control Units (ECU) together, mainly to reduce the amount of wiring that

would be required if hardwired integration were used.

Modern passenger cars contain many networks, which means that for the

architecture designer, there is an almost overwhelming number of choices on how to

design/partition the system depending on factors such as cost, weight, availability of

ECUs, safety, Electro-Magnetic Compatibility (EMC) etc. Despite the increasing role

played by in-vehicle networks in automotive electrical architectures, its design could

currently be described as a “black art”. Not only is there an almost overwhelming

number of choices facing the designer, but there is currently a lack of a quantifiable

process to aid decision making and there is a dearth of published literature available.

NetGen is a software tool used to design CAN/J1939, LIN and FlexRay

networks. For the product to remain competitive, it is desirable to have novel features

over the competition. This report describes a body of work, the aim of which was to

research in-vehicle network design processes, and to provide an improvement to such

processes. The opportunities of customer projects and availability of customer

information resulted in the scope of the research focusing on the adoption of LIN

technology and whether the adoption of it could reduce the cost and weight of the

target architecture. The research can therefore be seen to address two issues: firstly

the general problem of network designers needing to design in-vehicle network based

architectures balancing the needs of many design targets such as cost, weight etc, and

secondly the commercial motivation to find novel features for the design tool, NetGen. The outcome of the research described in this report was the development of

design processes that can be used for the selection of low cost and weight automotive

electrical architectures using coarse information, such as that which would be easily

available at the very beginning of a vehicle design programme. The key benefit of

this is that a number of candidate networked architectures can be easily assessed

candidates.mechanism: A CNN-BiLSTM-Attention hybrid network ingests synchronized voltage, current, and temperature measurements at the ECM harness connector, where CNN extracts local degradation features from the multi-physics signals, BiLSTM models their temporal evolution, and attention weighting isolates the signatures that govern terminal loosening, yielding a continuous aging-level estimate of the connection.
candidates.intervention: Instrument the ECM wiring harness connector terminals with voltage, current, and temperature sensing and apply the CNN-BiLSTM-Attention aging model to the recorded operating sequences to predict connection degradation state in service.

evidence_bundle.mechanism_source_span: By capturing voltage, current, and temperature parameters during low-voltage system operation, the model combines CNN's local feature extraction, BiLSTM's temporal sequence analysis, and attention mechanisms to predict aging levels.

warnings.mechanism: Capability collision test — keyword collision search is insufficient to establish novelty
warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

informational.mechanism: RES-4 narrow: adaptive transverse/sigmoid sinus stent for CSF absorption regulation via AG pressure gradient control
informational.lesson: MODEL-BOUNDED NEGATIVE RESULT: Before inventing variable geometry, calculate absolute pressure-control authority at the actual operating point. Relative r^4 sensitivity is meaningless if the absolute pressure drop is tiny. Under realistic post-stenting conditions (D=5-10mm, Q=200-500 mL/min), adaptive diameter control of a venous sinus produces <0.2 mmHg change in AG gradient — 5x below the 1 mmHg pre-registered threshold. Control authority exists only in the stenotic+high-flow regime (D≤4mm, Q≥1200 mL/min), which is incompatible with a stented patient whose stent has normalized diameter to 7-10mm. The network model (1323 configs) confirms: flow redistribution through contralateral sinus does NOT rescue control authority (dominance has no effect). NOT a universal vascular invariant — based on Poiseuille model with specific assumptions about geometry, flow, and topology.

informational.mechanism: Minimum Sufficient Validation Evidence Derivation (MSVED) — 4-link chain: ML change → clinical pathway → risk envelope → minimum sufficient evidence → sufficiency proof
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-019: A clinical-pathway-aware evidence selector must demonstrate that the clinical-pathway bridge produces a MATERIALLY DIFFERENT and BETTER evidence set than information-maximizing selection (BOED). If the pathway-aware selector uses MORE tests while achieving WORSE assurance, the clinical-pathway bridge adds complexity without value. The minimum-evidence claim must be validated by showing tests_required < BOED, not just tests_required < conventional. The killer experiment must compare against the STRONGEST available baseline (BOED), not just conventional full-validation.

informational.mechanism: Automated Sufficiency Proof Generator (CC-04 / MSES theorem) — formal proof that a specific evidence set E is sufficient to establish modification-specific clinical risk envelope R(Δ)
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-020: A sufficiency proof that is merely an integration of known statistical methods (NI testing + coverage + multiple-testing correction + sensitivity analysis) is NOT a novel mathematical result. Under §103, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is likely obvious (KSR v. Teleflex). The frontier is a NEW MATHEMATICAL BOUND — e.g., a tight bound on minimum evidence set size that is better than what existing methods give individually, or a proof technique that connects clinical pathway coverage to statistical sufficiency in a way that is not derivable from existing theory. Additionally: killer tests for sufficiency proofs must include a TRUE POSITIVE case (sufficient evidence for a SAFE modification that the system correctly accepts), not just a true negative (insufficient evidence that the system correctly rejects).

informational.mechanism: Non-Inferiority Statistical Engine (CC-08) — automated paired NI comparison with pre-registered margins for ML model modifications
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-021: Automating a standard statistical test (NI testing) for a regulatory context that explicitly requires it (PCCP) is NOT an invention. Under KSR, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is obvious. The coder correctly identified this in the R254 ranking ("NI testing is standard, high collision risk") but incorrectly chose to proceed. The CEO corrected: high collision risk is a RED FLAG, not a reason to proceed. Kill immediately if the smallest surviving mechanism is standard statistics + ML context + automated reporting.

informational.mechanism: SGET (Strain-Gated Electrochemical Transduction) — A=strain pulse changes B=electrochemical sensor from 2D surface to 3D depth profiling. First synergy-2 candidate.
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-022: Synergy ≠ novelty and synergy ≠ commercial moat. A functional interaction (A changes B) is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT for invention. The interaction itself — the causal law, the emergent effect, and functional equivalents across domains — must survive prior art independently. Additionally: synergy claims without quantitative comparison against the STRONGEST baseline are stories, not evidence. The unexpected-effect proof requires: (1) pre-registered quantitative prediction, (2) strongest baseline identified, (3) killer experiment vs that baseline, (4) result not predictable from A and B independently. The new standard: A changes B → unexpected effect → interaction survives prior art → reproducible advantage → cannot be cheaply reproduced → buyer value.

informational.mechanism: SC-05 Biofilm-Resistant Living-Surface Venous Interface — continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface with active surface-energy control at CSF-blood interface
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-023: A candidate that survives the 14-gate protocol at the CONCEPT level can be killed at the ELEMENT-DECOMPOSITION level. The 14 gates assessed M4 against the broad concept (continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface) and found M4=NOT FOUND. But deep collision revealed that each element (continuous renewal, dynamic topography, surface-energy modulation) is individually occupied by prior art. The combination is an aggregation of known anti-fouling approaches. The lesson: M4 must be assessed at the ELEMENT level, not the concept level. And M4=NOT FOUND means the search has not found comparable performance yet — not that it does not exist.

To address the challenge of predicting performance degradation caused by multi-physics coupling effects during wiring harness aging, this study proposes a CNN-BiLSTM-Attention hybrid neural network model. By capturing voltage, current, and temperature parameters during low-voltage system operation, the model combines CNN's local feature extraction, BiLSTM's temporal sequence analysis, and attention mechanisms to predict aging levels. Accelerated aging experiments were conducted to obtain wiring harnesses with different degradation levels from new to 720 h aged states, and a dedicated experimental platform was built for data collection and verification. The results show the system achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.02806, with 32.50% and 62.06% error reduction compared to LSTM and Random Forest models, respectively, demonstrating effective prediction performance.

custody_records.raw_content: Electrochemical batteries - essential to vehicle electrification and renewable energy storage - have ever-present reaction interfaces that require compromise among power, energy, lifetime, and safety. Here we report a chip-in-cell battery by integrating an ultrathin foil heater and a microswitch into the layer-by-layer architecture of a battery cell to harness intracell actuation and mutual thermal management between the heat-generating switch and heat-absorbing battery materials. The result is a two-terminal, drop-in ready battery with no bulky heat sinks or heavy wiring needed for an external high-power switch. We demonstrate rapid self-heating (∼ 60 °C min - 1 ), low energy consumption (0.138% °C - 1 of battery energy), and excellent durability (> 2000 cycles) of the greatly simplified chip-in-cell structure. The battery electronification platform unveiled here opens doors to include integrated-circuit chips inside energy storage cells for sensing, control, actuating, and wireless communications such that performance, lifetime, and safety of electrochemical energy storage devices can be internally regulated.

custody_records.raw_content: Commercialization of autonomous vehicle technology is a major goal of the automotive industry, thus research in this space is rapidly expanding across the world. However, despite this high level of research activity, literature detailing a straightforward and cost-effective approach to the development of an AV research platform is sparse. To address this need, we present the methodology and results regarding the AV instrumentation and controls of a 2019 Kia Niro which was developed for a local AV pilot program. This platform includes a drive-by-wire actuation kit, Aptiv electronically scanning radar, stereo camera, MobilEye computer vision system, LiDAR, inertial measurement unit, two global positioning system receivers to provide heading information, and an in-vehicle computer for driving environment perception and path planning. Robotic Operating System software is used as the system middleware between the instruments and the autonomous application algorithms. After selection, installation, and integration of these components, our results show successful utilization of all sensors, drive-by-wire functionality, a total additional power* consumption of 242.8 Watts (*Typical), and an overall cost of $118,189 USD, which is a significant saving compared to other commercially available systems with similar functionality. This vehicle continues to serve as our primary AV research and development platform.

custody_records.raw_content: This manuscript presents a control barrier function based approach to shared control for preventing a vehicle from entering the part of the state space where it is unrecoverable. The maximal phase recoverable ellipse is presented as a safe set in the sideslip angle--yaw rate phase plane where the vehicle's state can be maintained. An exponential control barrier function is then defined on the maximal phase recoverable ellipse to promote safety. Simulations demonstrate that this approach enables safe drifting, that is, driving at the handling limit without spinning out. Results are then validated for shared control drifting with an experimental vehicle in a closed course. The results show the ability of this shared control formulation to maintain the vehicle's state within a safe domain in a computationally efficient manner, even in extreme drifting maneuvers.

custody_records.raw_content: Vehicle platooning has been shown to be quite fruitful in the transportation industry to enhance fuel economy, road throughput, and driving comfort. Model Predictive Control (MPC) is widely used in literature for platoon control to achieve certain objectives, such as safely reducing the distance among consecutive vehicles while following the leader vehicle. In this paper, we propose a Distributed Nonlinear MPC (DNMPC), based upon an existing approach, to control a heterogeneous dynamic platoon with unidirectional topologies, handling possible cut-in/cut-out maneuvers. The introduced method addresses a collision-free driving experience while tracking the desired speed profile and maintaining a safe desired gap among the vehicles. The time of convergence in the dynamic platooning is derived based on the time of cut-in and/or cut-out maneuvers. In addition, we analyze the improvement level of driving comfort, fuel economy, and absolute and relative convergence of the method by using distributed metric learning and distributed optimization with Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM). Simulation results on a dynamic platoon with cut-in and cut-out maneuvers and with different unidirectional topologies show the effectiveness of the introduced method.
